title: At-home LED masks for facial rejuvenation: an October 2026 systematic review
headline: A systematic review of at-home LED devices found 8 studies (365 participants) with improvements in wrinkles, texture and elasticity, mostly with red and near-infrared light; protocols varied widely and diverse skin phenotypes were underrepresented.
evidenceTier: Systematic review of 8 studies (abstract read; PubMed search only)
fit: Partial. It supports red and near-infrared at-home light for ageing signs in general terms; it does not settle blue-light safety in pigment-prone skin, which the abstract does not address.
displaces: Fits nowhere new if a home LED device is already in use; it would replace, not add to, an existing device.
estimateNote: Prices marked EST are my guesses, not looked up.
summaryPoints: Abstract (read): MEDLINE/PubMed-only search; 8 randomized, split-face or prospective cohort studies of at-home LED devices, 365 participants; wavelengths 440 to 1072 nm, red and near-infrared most common.
Reported: statistically significant improvements in wrinkles, texture, elasticity and periorbital lines with high satisfaction; adverse events infrequent, mild and transient.
Authors' caveats: variable protocols, limited comparative data, underrepresentation of diverse skin phenotypes. A single-database search can miss studies; full text not opened.
toneData: Underrepresentation of diverse skin phenotypes (authors' statement)
fitLine: Supports red and near-infrared in general; says nothing specific about deep skin or blue light.
timeline: Study durations vary; not extracted from the abstract

fitAxes.why: Blue-light acne use not addressed in the abstract.
